To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“Submarine discontinuity surfaces can be distinguished from subaerial surfaces by their vertical and lateral relationships, their associated rock sequences, and by their regional setting.”
(a) the Edwards Formation was deposited on the sea floor, (b) it was never exposed above the water table, and (c) its discontinuity surfaces were never subaerially exposed.

(1) discontinuity surfaces that are interpreted as subaerial in origin are commonly submarine in origin, (2) the presence of submarine discontinuity surfaces in a stratigraphic section can be determined from a combination of field observations, laboratory studies and geologic history, and (3) discontinuity surfaces of submarine origin are more common in carbonate rocks than previously thought.

the interpretation of carbonate rock sequences, particularly those of the Cretaceous Edwards Formation of Texas.
the origin, recognition, and interpretation of discontinuity (or “hardground”) surfaces in the Cretaceous Edwards Formation of Texas.
the recognition and interpretation of submarine versus subaerial discontinuities in ancient carbonates.

discontinuity surfaces are best interpreted as subaerial if: (1) the surface is a regional erosional unconformity, (2) the surface is overlain by a regional transgressive unit, and/or (3) the rock sequence above and below the surface shows marked differences in sedimentation and/or cementation.

the interpretation of discontinuity surface type is a key factor in determining how to interpret and map carbonate sequences.
